The slender loris (Loris tardigradus) is a small, nocturnal strepsirrhine primate endemic to the tropical forests of Sri Lanka. Neonates of this species are born weighing approximately 11 grams [Wwb = approximately 11 grams], a relatively modest mass for a lorisid primate. This low birth mass reflects the altricial nature of the young, which rely heavily on maternal care and a prolonged period of lactation. Typically, a female gives birth to a single offspring per reproductive event, and field observations indicate that she may produce up to 1.3 litters per year under optimal conditions, yielding a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 1.95 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 1.95 offspring per year] that is constrained by the energetic demands of gestation and extended maternal investment. The species exhibits low fecundity relative to many other mammals of comparable adult body mass, a pattern consistent with a slow-paced life history strategy.

Gestation in the slender loris lasts approximately 166 days [tg = approximately 166 days] when the mother maintains a typical core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This relatively protracted gestation period, compared to other strepsirrhines of similar size, suggests a significant investment in prenatal development. Following birth, the neonatal period involves continuous physical contact with the mother, who carries her young on her ventral surface. The long gestation and subsequent dependency phase are thought to be adaptations to a diet of small animal prey, which provides a relatively constant but energy-dense nutritional base, allowing females to sustain the metabolic costs of extended pregnancy and lactation. Variation in gestation length may be influenced by maternal nutritional condition, but the figure of 166 days at the species' normothermic temperature represents a well-documented baseline.

The period of maternal dependence after birth is substantial. Weaning, marking the nutritional independence of the young from milk, occurs approximately 150 days after birth [tx = approximately 150 days after birth] under standard thermoregulatory conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. At this point, the weanling has attained a body mass of about 139 grams [Wwx = about 139 grams], representing a significant increase from birth mass but still only about 58% of the ultimate adult weight. The long weaning period is characteristic of lorisids and allows the juvenile to develop the complex predatory and locomotor skills necessary for an arboreal, insectivorous lifestyle. Juveniles begin to capture small invertebrate prey during the later stages of lactation but remain reliant on maternal milk for a significant portion of their early energetic requirements. This gradual dietary transition minimizes the risk of starvation and facilitates a steady growth trajectory.

Under typical thermoregulatory conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the onset of reproductive capability is delayed to approximately 380 days after birth [tp = approximately 380 days after birth], allowing an extended juvenile period for the development of foraging, territorial defense, and social skills before the individual begins to breed. The ultimate adult wet weight for the slender loris is recorded at approximately 238.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 238.2 grams], a size that is not typically achieved until well after the onset of puberty and that places this species within the typical range for lorisids, reflecting the energetic demands of an insectivorous diet. The substantial growth trajectory from the 11 gram neonate to the adult state underscores the considerable time and energetic resources required to reach full physical maturity and reproductive potential.

The slender loris has a relatively long lifespan for a primate of its small body size. Maximum longevity in the wild is estimated at nearly 19.5 years [am = nearly 19.5 years], a duration that underscores the species' slow life history pace under its typical core temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This extended lifespan is a hallmark of a "slow" life history, characterized by low fecundity, prolonged gestation and infancy, delayed maturation, and low adult mortality rates. The ultimate total body length typically ranges from approximately 15 to 25 centimeters (15-25 centimeters) [Li = 15-25 centimeters], a compact, elongated frame well-suited to an arboreal existence that facilitates efficient movement through the dense canopy in pursuit of insect prey. The slender loris is also notable for its strong grip and slow climbing movements, which aid in stealthy foraging.
